result.competitor: I found no Bahamas-specific software and no public online register or portal; the process is paper-based at the ministry. Generic international guard-management software already does the core tracking job: Guardhouse (licence and certification tracking with renewal alerts; its automated licence checks are UK-only), TrackTik (licence tracking with renewal alerts), and OctopusPro (scheduling and invoicing). None of them files the Bahamian renewal itself, but the reminder and roster-compliance part is covered.
result.duty: Inquiry Agents and Security Guards Act (the industry also calls it the Private Security Act 1970). The company and every guard must each hold a separate licence from the Minister of National Security. Guards must be Bahamian citizens, with an exception for spousal-permit holders. Licences are annual, run 1 Jan to 31 Dec, and must be renewed each year. While police vet the applicant, a temporary licence covers up to 3 months. Fees: guard $10 (Tribune 2024); firm licence BS$500 a year and temporary BS$125 every 3 months (unofficial wikiprocedure page). Hiring unlicensed or non-Bahamian guards brings fines of $500-$2,000 (Tribune, undated). Firms also need indemnity insurance. In June-July 2026 the ministry cracked down on unlicensed providers and unpaid fees, and planned amendments (tougher penalties, training standards, a new magstripe guard licence card) have no dates and are not passed. I found no recurring return beyond the licence renewal. I could not open the Act's text on the official laws portal.
result.market: I found no official count. The Tribune's "12,000 security firms" figure is implausible for a population of about 400k and is unsourced. The ministry removed 150 inactive firms and 200 unauthorised guards and collected more than $156k in fees. At roughly $500 per firm plus $10 per guard, that suggests a few hundred licensed firms at most, with thousands of guards in total. The market is very small, and the reachable buyers are probably 100-300 firms. Client-side guard checking would need a public register, and none exists.
result.reason: The duty is real, but I'm scoring it low. Under the Inquiry Agents and Security Guards Act (the industry calls it the Private Security Act 1970), each security company and each of its guards needs its own Ministry of National Security licence. Licences are annual and expire 31 December, after 3-month temporary licences while police vet the applicant. Guard licences reportedly cost $10; a firm licence is about $500 (wiki, unofficial). Hiring unlicensed or non-Bahamian guards brings $500-$2,000 fines. The 2026 crackdown shows enforcement is happening. However, the workflow is a simple paper renewal once a year, and the market is tiny: the ministry collected only about $156k in fees, so there are probably a few hundred firms, not 12,000. Generic guard software (Guardhouse, TrackTik) already tracks licence expiry. I found nothing Bahamas-specific, and the amendments are undated.

The 2004 Act's licensing duty is real. The Tribune of 12 Mar 2026 reports the 2026 Bill only as proposed. It would set a $5,000 fine plus $100/day for non-compliant staff, double renewal fee if unpaid by January, annual staff medical certificates and conviction checks. Searches found no sign it has passed or taken effect, so the new duties are unconfirmed. No competing software or state portal turned up, but coverage was thin. Market is small: 118 private pre-schools were in the 2022 voucher programme, and no register total was found. The buyers are micro-operators with low software budgets, and a tracker is only a simple reminder and checklist. High risk of low willingness to pay.

The duty is real. The Commercial Recreational Watercraft Act (Cap. 278A) and its Regulations require craft registration, a Port Department safety inspection certificate, and operator licences. Failure carries a fine and/or prison. The Boat Registration Act also applies. A 2021 government notice says the Port Department already runs an online service (bahamas.gov.bs/port) covering vessel registration, captain's licence and foreign charter licence. I found no private vendor. The score is low because the state portal covers the core job, the operator count is likely a few hundred, and annual frequency means little recurring pain. Not checked: current renewal dates, fees and operator count. The Act text and handbook were not opened.

Duty is partly real: Hotels Act 1970 licensing through the Hotel Licensing Department, plus free DIR vacation-rental registration since 1 Mar 2023 (ewnews). Not verified: the 2026 enforcement drive (only the bnbcalc blog says so). Also unverified: STVR fee, renewal cycle and penalties. The tourismtoday fees page covers hotels only. A DIR official said there is no new legislation, and about 20% of 20,000+ properties are registered. I found no Bahamas-specific compliance software, but the search was thin. The free DIR portal and the one-off, simple registration limit recurring value. VAT rate conflict (10% vs 12%) unresolved. Market is large but fragmented and hard to reach. Weak sources overall.
